paras.t: This question appeared to be unexpectedly challenging to many candidates, with the majority failing to identify the organelle as a chloroplast. Most candidates achived one mark for stating that prokaryotic cells do not have membrane-bound organelles. The first example below shows a 2 mark answer that identifies the organelle as membrane-bound, and stating that prokaryotic cells do not have membrane-bound organelles. However, a high number of candidates lost both marks for identifying the organelle as a nucleus and then continuing along this line, stating that prokaryotic cells do not store their DNA in the nucleus, but in the cytoplasm. The second example shows such a response, which received 0 marks.

This question required candidates to measure the image size and to use the magnification equation to calculate the actual size of the image, giving their final answer in micrometres. The majority of candidates scored both marks, however many candidates lost a mark for incorrectly converting the millimetres to micrometres, often as a consequence of measuring in centimetre and not millimetres.
This multiple choice question was well answered by candidates. Most were able to identify the structures in the electron micrograph and correctly selected option C.
This multiple choice question was also very well answered. A few more incorrect responses than 1bi, with B being the most common incorrect response.

This multiple choice question was well answered by candidates, who showed a good understanding of the word ‘endemic’ and the vast majority selected option B. A small proportion selected other options, with option D being the most common incorrect answer.
Candidates performed well on this multiple choice question, showing a good understanding of adaptations. The vast majority selected the correct answer of C.

This 5 mark question asked candidates to apply their knowledge of the process of natural selection to an unfamiliar organism. Overall, candidates performed well on this question, with most gaining at least 3 marks. The first example shows a 4 mark response, where the candidate gained credit for mentioning genetic variation, and for stating that individuals with the advantageous characteristics were more likely to survive and reproduce and pass on those alleles to offspring, leading to a change in allele frequency. The candidate missed a mark for not giving a relevant example of the adaptation, or mentioning an example of a selection pressure.

Candidates mainly failed to get marking point 1 due to not including the word ‘genetic’ when describing variation. Others mentioned mutations, but did not link this to new alleles being formed or to genetic variation, and therefore missed out on that mark. An example of this is shown in the answer below, which was awarded 3 marks.
The example below shows a good, 5 mark response.

This question was not well answered by the majority of candidates, with many simply stating that organs are a group of tissues, without specifying that they are made of different tissues, and therefore losing the mark.
This multiple choice question was answered well by candidates, although a small proportion thought that only xylem contains lignin, with a surprising number of candidates also selecting option A.
Candidates performed well on this question, with many being awarded 3 or 4 marks. The first example below shows a good 4 mark response for correctly linking the structure of xylem to its function.

Many candidates lost MP3 for simply stating that the xylem is lignified but failing to specify that the lignin is in the xylem walls. Other candidates wrote about the xylem being made up of dead cells and providing descriptions of this, which gained no credit – the important feature being the lack of cytoplasm. The example below shows a 2 mark response where the candidate has made both of these mistakes.

This question was well answered by candidates, with the majority gaining full marks. A significant proportion of candidates wrote about leaves being biodegradable, not filling up landfill sites which did not gain any credit in the context of sustainability. Furthermore, some candidates went into detail about oil-based platics leading to global warming and climate change, which was not the context of the question.

Most candidates achieved MP2 and recognised that members of the same species interbreed to produce fertile offspring, but many candidates did not appreciate that members of the same species also have similar characteristics, and therefore did not achieve MP1. It should also be noted that a few responses included the word inbreeding instead of interbreeding, and therefore lost MP2.

This question was overall well answered by candidates, with many recognising that species richness is the number of different species in an area, and that a higher species richness would indicate a higher biodiversity. The example below shows such a 2 mark answer.
Very few candidates appreciated the need to count the number of species in the same sized area of the two habitats, and therefore MP2 was rarely awarded.

This calculation question assessed whether candidates can interpret and use the index of biodiversity equation. Most candidates scored both marks for the correct answer of 5.94. The most common mistakes were candidates ignoring the Σ sign and therefore calculating the incorrect denominator, or failing to round their answer to 2 decimal places as instructed.

Generally, candidates did not perform well on this question, with many answers lacking in detail. Many were unable to distinguish between the information that index of diversity provides and how it differs from species richness, with many candidates gaining 1 mark for stating that index of diversity takes into account species evenness or abundance. Many candidates lost MP1 for failing to be specific about why species richness is limited, and some candidates lost marks for implying that population refers to members of multiple species. The first example below shows a response that gained no marks for lack of detail.
The second example above shows a response that gained 1 mark for mentioning that index of difersity includes the proportion of individuals.

This question proved challenging for candidates, with many struggling to express in words what is meant by the term ‘continuous variation ’. Most candidates gained 1 mark for mentioning a good example of continuous variation, with height being the most common. A significant proportion of candidates wrote about continuous variation being caused by multiple genes or being a combination of genetics and the environment, which gained no credit.

This question discriminated well between candidates, with many gaining 1 or 2 marks for mentioning multiple genes being involved from different loci. Only a small number of candidates went on to describe how these multiple genes each have a small effect on the phenotype, and even fewer stated that the effects are cumulative, so MP3 and MP4 were rarely seen. MP5 was more frequently awarded, with some gaining credit for being specific about the different shades of eye colour being caused by polygenic inheritance. Once again, candidates gained no credit for mentioning the effects of the environment. Some candidates used the word ‘alleles’ instead of genes. The first example below shows a 2 mark response where the candidate gained MP1 and MP2, however even though they mentioned eye colour, the lack of specificity meant that MP5 could not be awarded. The second example shows a better, 3 mark response from a candidate.

This question discriminated well between candidates. Most candidates were awarded MP1, though some had difficulties articulating this point. Many candidates were also awarded MP5 for correctly interpreting the data and stating that 58% of dogs had normal hip joints. The next most commonly awarded marking point was MP2, especially in answers that already had MP1. The first example shows a 2 mark answer that includes MP1 and MP2. However, only the highest scoring candidates were able to identify the recessive nature of the alleles, or that the severity of the disorder is linked to the number of alleles present. A small number of candidates included 42% in their data, but could not be awarded MP4 because they did not link this to the commonality of the allele in the gene pool. Few candidates gained full 4 marks for this question. A 3 mark response is shown as the second example below.
Most candidates were awarded the mark to this multiple choice question, with A being the most common incorrect answer.

Many candidates were awarded the mark here, but a small proportion chose B instead of C, which showed some candidates had difficulties interpreting the question or applying their knowledge of gene expression to an unfamiliar context.
This question proved deceptively difficult for candidates, as the options had similar wording. This caught some candidates out, with all three incorrect options seen.

This question produced a range of responses from candidates, proving challenging to many. Many candidates could not be awarded MP1 because they mentioned the armadillos being genetically identical, which was already mentioned in the question stem, and therefore could gain no credit. Most candidates only achieved 1 mark, with MP2 being far more common than MP1. A small number of responses mentioned ethics or the idea of armadillos being similar to humans, which were not relevant comments.

This question about the effects of DNA methylation on gene expression was answered very well, with most candidates scoring at least 2 marks. Most candidates showed a good understanding of DNA methylation and its effects on deactivating a gene. The first example shows a good 3 mark response.

Some responses lost marks due to candidares being unsure as to whether DNA methylation activates or deactivates a gene. Other responses lacked detail, with some candidates failing to mention where the methyl groups attach, or which molecule is prevented from attaching to the DNA/promoter. The least seen marking point was MP2, which showed candidates were still unsure as to how methylation changes the DNA arrangement around the histone proteins. The second example below shows a 1 mark response, where only MP1 could be awarded.

This question proved more difficult than intended, with very few candidates achieving full marks. MP1 was awarded most often, showing that candidates understood the data and the experiment, with fewer scoring MP2 for correctly deducing that methyl groups must have deactivated the agouti gene, resulting in offspring with brown fur. A high number of candidates did not score MP2, or more than 1 mark, because they referred to the brown gene being activated or deactivated. It was clearly stated in the question that the brown gene is always switched on, therefore candidates must appreciate the details within the experiment and must ensure that they carefully read all parts of the question to avoid losing marks unneccesarily. The example below shows a 1 mark response, which contained the aforementioned misconceptions.

Some candidates were able to deduce the effects of the methylation of the agouti gene on the health of the mice. Some attempts were made and candidates did suggest that methyl groups affect the health, but the mark was not awarded for omitting to state that it is the methylation of the agouti gene
that affects health. The example below shows a good 3
mark response.

Overall candidates found this question conceptually difficult, although it was assessing an aspect of the specification. The most frequent mark awarded was for MP2, with MP1 rarely being awarded. This showed candidates did not take into account the fact they had been previously informed that the mothers all had the same starting phenotype, and therefore the only change was the diet they were being fed. The example below shows a response which was awarded MP1.

This question produced good responses from most candidates, with many being awarded full marks. Candidates mainly lost MP2, for suggesting that mitochondria ‘ produce energy ’ rather than ‘ produce ATP ’ or ‘ release energy ’ . MP3 was not awarded to some candidates for failing to specify that enzymes from the acrosome break down the zona pellucida. A 3 mark response is shown below. Ideally, candidates should refer to the energy being used to move the flagellum.

The investigation, coupled with the graph, was not well understood by candidates. This was evident with many candidates second guessing themselves, many wrote the correct conclusion only to cross it out and replace it with an incorrect deduction. The majority of candidates scored MP2, for correctly identifying that the drug increases the number of sperm cells with fully reacted acrosomes, but assumed that would increase fertility and not decrease it as they interpreted the data incorrectly, not realising that if the acrosome had already reacted there would be no enzyme to break down the zona pellucida, hence decreasing fertility. This misunderstanding prevented candidates from achieving some of the marks. Below is a 2 mark example that was awarded MP2 and MP3, but contained the common misconception concerning fertility.
The example below shows one of the few instances where a candidate has understood the effect of sildenafil on sperm cells, and therefore scored 3 marks.

This question required candidates to draw a suitable graph on the grid provided, plotting data from a table. Selecting the correct graph for the data, drawing suitable, linear scales, including correct labels with units, having correct lines drawn and including labels, continues to be a challenging combination of skills for candidates to master. A surprisingly small proportion of candidates were awarded the full 4 marks for the correct line graph, and an example is shown below.

Many candidates were capped at a maximum of 3 marks because they chose to draw a bar graph instead, despite being provided with numerical data best displayed in a line graph. This prevented them from achieving the mark for linear scales. An example is shown below.
Other mistakes included incorrect scales, or labels without units. The example below shows a graph that lost a mark due to an incorrectly labelled x axis.

This question produced a wide range of responses, with many candidates being awarded 1 or 2 marks. MP2 and MP4 were by far the most frequent marks awarded, showing that most candidates were able to compare the results with the control and provide a link to the function of the mitochondria. Fewer candidates were then able to link the function of the mitochondria to an improved function of the flagellum leading to a higher velocity. It should be noted that candidates must be specific when interpreting data, and they should give specific values rather than generic responses. MP1 was a straightforward mark that could not always be given for this very reason, with many candidates suggesting that sildenafil increased velocity of sperm cells, without referring to the relevant time range - from 0 to 30 minutes. The example below shows a concise, 4 mark response that achieved what most failed, in discussing the results of the investigation in relation to mitochondrial function.

This question was very well answered by candidates, with many scoring full marks for correctly identifying germination and microbial growh as being stopped by the drying of seeds. MP1 was rarely mentioned, but MP2 and MP3 were very common. A small number of candidates made generic references, such as drying prevents seed growth rather than germination.

This question assessed the effect of temperature on bacteria and many responses gained credit for the basic point that increasing temperature increases bacterial growth. MP4 was slightly less common, with few relating enzyme acitivty to kinetic energy, with more picking up on the denaturation of enzymes at high temperatures for MP5. A surprising number of candidates thought that enzymes denature at low temperatures and therefore gained no credit. A worrying number of responses did not even refer to enzyme activity, with many stating that bacteria denature or that bacteria themselves gain more kinetic energy, rather than enzymes and substrates. The first example shows a 1 mark response while the second example shows a 3 mark response.

This question produced a wide range of responses, but generally it was well answered, with the modal mark being 2. Most candidates recognised that the leaves had the highest antimicrobial properties due to having the largest zone of inhibition. Those responses that were not awarded the first 2 marks had MP2 but did not link it to the antimicrobial properties or they had MP1, but did not phrase correctly the idea of the largest zone of inhibition. The example shown below is a typical 2 mark response, where MP1 and MP2 were both awarded.
A significant number of candidates spotted that there was no significant difference between the fruit and the seeds, because their ranges overlapped. Below is an example of a 3 mark response.

This question asked candidates to design an investigation to measure the impact of the storage time for coffee seeds on their antimicrobial properties. The candidates had to include a valid method, describing in detail how the independent variable should be changed, how the dependent variable would be measured and standardised, and how controlled variables would be kept constant.

This 6 mark question discriminated well between candidates, with a range of responses from Level 1 to Level 3. The majority of responses were Level 1 and Level 2 in almost equal proportions. However many were unable to reach a Level 3 response due to a lack in detail regarding the preparation of an extract from the seeds (many putting whole seeds on the agar), or how to use aseptic techniques when handling bacterial cultures. Those responses that were awarded Level 3, were, for the most part, given 5 marks and not 6. Some responses were lacking in detail regarding how the variables should be changed, measured or controlled. Many candidates simply stated variables, without giving detail on how
these variables are manipulated (techniques,
measurements, equipment).

The example below shows a Level 1, 2 mark response. The reason this response was awarded Level 1 is that it lacked sufficient detail of the method, but it included points about the variables, especially around measuring the antimicrobial properties.

The responses that were awarded Level 2, had a good level of detail on either the preparation of the extract or demonstrated a sound understanding of aseptic techniques in order to inoculate bacteria on the agar plates. Their method had a few missing details, such as valid comparisons and details on the zones of inhibition, but overall the method could potentially lead to valid outcomes. The examples below show two Level 2 responses. The first was awarded 4 marks, and the second was awarded 3 marks.

The highest scoring candidates were able to access Level 3 by demonstrating a wide array of knowledge regarding the preparation of the extract and placing it on a paper disc, the inoculation of bacteria onto the agar jelly (many referred to either agar or bacteria and not both), with detailed presentation of how aseptic techniques would prevent contamination of the agar plates, as well as further details on how validity of results would be assured, such as using statistical tests. Almost no candidates mentioned statistical tests, which would be very useful in an investigation such as this. Below is a Level 3 answer that was awarded 5 marks.
This paper tested the knowledge, understanding and application of material from Topic 3: Voice of the Genome and Topic 4: Biodiversity and Natural Resources.
The range of questions provided opportunity for candidates to demonstrate their grasp of these topics and apply their knowledge to unfamiliar contexts.

The questions on this paper yielded a wide range of responses and some very good answers were seen. The paper appears to have worked very well with all questions achieving the full range of marks available. There were some straightforward questions that were answered well in the majority of cases and some more challenging questions that discriminated well. Candidates in this year have shown a greater appreciation for the need to address the context of the question instead of producing generic responses, however a small number of candidates were applying their generally extensive knowledge to the wrong context, which shows they were not reading the question fully.

Questions that required recall of factual information were generally well answered, as were the majority of the calculation questions, however a number of candidates were not precise in using the correct terminology and therefore lost marks.

Candidates still struggled with interpreting data from various graphs and tables, with many candidates losing marks for simply stating data, instead of manipulating the data. Furthermore, graph drawing was a skill that many candidates still lost marks on, emphasising the need for further practice on scientific drawings, drawing tables and graphs.

This year saw many more candidates than usual opt for using extra paper. It should be noted that candidates can and should write on any of the blank spaces around their answers, as all of that space is scanned and visible to examiners. Candidates are encouraged to be more concise and precise with their answers to extended writing questions, as those who wrote on extra paper did not necessarily achieve more of the marking points.

Candidates are encouraged to not cross out any answers unless they can replace them with a better answer. This year has also seen a few correct points being crossed out. For extended writing responses involving the design of an experimental procedure, candidates are advised to number their steps to allow a clearer order of events to be more easily and logically sequenced.
